meta.regime: The global tightening impulse identified yesterday has now claimed its last holdout. For a fortnight the franc was the one G10 currency where the energy shock produced nothing - six consecutive haven tests failed, CPI at 0.4% and falling, an SNB explicitly discussing negative rates. This morning's 0.8% print, double the July rate and above every forecast including TE's own 0.6%, closes that gap: seven of eight G10 central banks are now facing an inflation impulse their models did not have in June, and the market has moved the whole board to a tightening footing against a dollar whose data has missed three sessions running. The important nuance is that the currencies being paid are the ones where the CENTRAL BANK has spoken, not the ones where the data is hottest - Japan has the lowest headline CPI on this board at 1.9% and the strongest currency, because Ueda put September live and the market moved to 85-90%. New Zealand has the highest at 4.1% and is the weakest, because the RBNZ said it would look through it. Underneath, the oil market has begun to decouple from the headlines: the US struck Iranian tankers for the first time and crude still fell.

dailyRead: The one thing this file has been waiting a fortnight for happened at 06:30Z and it went the other way from the base case. Swiss August CPI printed 0.8% year-on-year against a 0.5% market consensus, a 0.6% TE forecast and 0.4% in July - the fastest rate since August 2024 - with core inflation up to 0.4% from 0.3%, its first increase of the entire year, and the monthly rate turning positive at 0.1% after -0.1%. Yesterday's file explicitly pre-committed that a print at or below 0.4% takes the franc to -1 and that 0.6% with a positive monthly rate would be its first genuine two-sided risk in a fortnight. It got neither; it got a beat well beyond both scenarios, and the tape confirmed it inside the hour - USD/CHF fell 0.47% to 0.80913, the largest single move on the board today and the first time in six sessions the franc has been bought on a signal of its own rather than left behind. CHF is UPGRADED from 0 to +1. But be precise about what the upgrade is and is not. The Federal Statistical Office attributes the pickup mainly to higher petroleum costs and the weaker franc pushing up imported goods prices, with clothing and footwear falling - this is the energy shock arriving in Switzerland with a two-month lag, not Swiss domestic demand. At 0.8% headline and 0.4% core, inflation sits in the lower half of the SNB's 0-2% target band; the Bank has signalled it could cut BELOW zero if necessary and officials still expect the policy rate to remain at zero through 2027; TE carries a 0% consensus for September 24 and a Reuters poll unanimously expects zero held through the year. So the correct trade is removing the automatic short-franc leg from every cross, not adding a hawkish-SNB long. That is why CHF goes to +1 and not higher, and why the CHF crosses drop to MEDIUM conviction rather than being flipped outright. The yen did the opposite of the franc and did it with the central bank's full backing. USD/JPY broke through 158 and then 157 to trade at 157.016, down 1.07% on the day and 1.49% on the week, and the pricing behind it has hardened materially: the market now puts 85-90% odds on a 25 basis point BoJ hike to 1.25% at the September 17-18 meeting, up from the 'live meeting' framing this file used yesterday. Three things drove that. Ueda said the Bank will consider a rate hike at EVERY policy meeting including this month's and that he will decide with upside price risks in mind, naming the Middle East conflict, AI-related demand and weak-yen pass-through. Takata, the lone July dissenter for 1.25%, renewed his push for consecutive hikes. And US Treasury Secretary Bessent publicly urged Ueda to take decisive monetary steps to combat yen weakness - which is the July 31 joint intervention being escalated into policy pressure, and it removes the last argument for fading the move. The 10-year JGB at 3.02% is the highest since 1996. JPY is UPGRADED from +1 to +2 and is now the strongest currency on this board. The honest caveat from yesterday still stands and has not improved: Japan imports essentially all its oil, the trade balance is MINUS 634 billion yen and the current account swung to MINUS 923 billion, so this is a policy-expectations rally sitting on top of a deteriorating terms of trade. Household spending prints tomorrow at 02:30Z and average cash earnings plus final Q2 GDP on September 8 are what confirm or break the wage-price case. Against those two upgrades the dollar simply kept leaking. There was no new US data overnight - ISM services lands at 14:00Z with prices paid consensus 66 after 70.3, jobless claims at 12:30Z - and DXY is 99.267, down 0.33%, having lost ground to the franc, the yen, the euro, the kiwi and the loonie in the same session. The three misses that produced yesterday's downgrade are unchanged: ADP +38,000 against 47,000 expected and the weakest since January, ISM manufacturing 54.6 against 55.2, JOLTS 7.271 million against 7.3 million. USD stays at 0 and tomorrow's payroll is the resolving event; note that Reuters' median has drifted to +55,000 against the +58,000 consensus this file has been carrying, and wage growth is seen slowing to 2.9% from 3.2% - the softer of the two framings. The oil market deserves the most attention because it decoupled from its own headlines today. The escalation was the largest of the war so far: US forces struck Iranian oil tankers for the FIRST time, hitting roughly 100 targets on Tuesday under a new 'tanker for tanker' policy approved by Trump, in retaliation for IRGC attacks on commercial shipping and on American bases. A tanker was struck by three projectiles 17 nautical miles east of Khasab on August 31 and two supertankers were hit off Oman on Monday night. And WTI still FELL 1.12% to 89.994, with Brent down 1.20% to 94.485. The week is still up 7.74% and the month 18.77%, so the risk premium has not gone - but the marginal barrel is no longer responding to marginal escalation, which fits the US Energy Secretary's claim that over 17 million barrels a day transited on Tuesday, the highest since the conflict began. For FX this matters in two places. It caps the CAD story rather than breaking it: USD/CAD is 1.38263, down only 0.11% today after yesterday's 0.36%, so the loonie is consolidating the Macklem move rather than extending it. And it removes the cleanest argument for pressing USOIL longs at these levels. CAD stays at +2 on the strength of the central bank rather than the commodity - Macklem's 'if it takes more than one increase, we're prepared to do that' is still the single most explicit hawkish pre-commitment on this board, and Q2 GDP at 3.3% annualised is the best growth number in the G10. The other three currencies did nothing that changes their scores. The euro holds +2 at 1.16072, up 0.16%, with the September 10 deposit-facility hike to 2.50% from 2.25% fully priced and HICP at 3.3%, the highest since September 2023; Lagarde has flagged that she is watching second-round effects and expects inflation well above target into H1 2027, but core easing to 2.4% below consensus with services at 3.0% is why this is +2 and not +3, and why Lane's speech tomorrow at 09:00Z is a genuine risk - a one-and-done framing takes the euro off +2 quickly. The Aussie holds +2 at 0.71673, essentially unchanged today, on the strongest fundamental package on the board: the G10-high cash rate at 4.35%, Q2 GDP at +0.4% q/q against +0.3% expected with annual growth 2.1% against 1.8%, trimmed mean inflation stuck at 3.6% and September hike pricing at 57% from 48%. Sterling holds 0 at 1.34985, up 0.09% but still down 0.70% on the week and now the funding leg against four currencies rather than a view in its own right - Bank Rate 3.75%, held 6-3 on July 30 with Pill, Greene and Mann voting for 4.00%, core CPI flat at 2.6% for a third month, and nothing before Bailey and the DMP survey tomorrow at 08:50Z. And the kiwi holds 0 at 0.58591, up 0.16% today after being the worst major of the week at -1.53%; the RBNZ hiked to 2.75% and then published a track reaching only 2.81% in December, which the market read as looking through a 4.1% inflation rate it explicitly blamed on Middle East fuel prices. That is the sharpest illustration of today's regime: the highest inflation on the board buys you nothing if your central bank says it will ignore it. Precious metals were firm without being dramatic - gold 4,423.54 up 0.81% but still down 3.85% on the week, silver 65.778 up 0.71% and down 5.02% on the week, copper 6.4952 down 0.09% and 1.43% on the week with the China input still soft. Practically, the board now has four currencies at +2, which means the cleanest trades are no longer between the strong currencies but from the three zeroes into them: short USD/JPY, GBP/JPY, NZD/JPY, USD/CAD, GBP/CAD, NZD/CAD, and long AUD/NZD and EUR/NZD. The CHF crosses that were free money for a fortnight are now two-sided and should be sized down accordingly. Size down everything oil-linked and everything Canada-linked into tomorrow's 12:30Z double print.

The case: August flash HICP 3.3%, up from 2.9% and the highest since September 2023, with inflation MoM +0.4%; TE macro re-verified as Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, unemployment 6.4%, manufacturing PMI 52.7 from 51.9, services 51.7, consumer confidence -15.5, retail sales -0.3% m/m, trade balance back to +8,600 million and the current account to +46.9 billion. Most analysts expect the 25bp move on September 10 with a further hike later this year a distinct possibility. The caveat that keeps this at +2 rather than +3 is unchanged and is the thing to watch: core eased to 2.4%, BELOW the 2.5% consensus, with services at 3.0%, so the energy surge has not yet passed into underlying prices - the ECB's own test is failing even as the headline forces its hand, which makes September look like the last hike of the cycle rather than the first of a run. EUR/USD is 1.16072 and up 0.16% today but still DOWN 0.39% on the week with the hike fully priced, so the euro's edge is against the kiwi and sterling, not the dollar. geopolitics: This week produced the largest escalation of the war so far and the smallest price reaction, and that divergence is the most important thing on the oil page today. US forces struck Iranian oil tankers for the FIRST time, hitting roughly 100 targets on Tuesday under a new 'tanker for tanker' policy approved by Trump, in explicit retaliation for IRGC attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait and on American bases in the region. That followed a tanker being struck by three unknown projectiles seventeen nautical miles east of Khasab, Oman, on August 31, and two supertankers - the Bahri VLCC Sidr and Sinokor's Senegal Prosperity - being hit off Oman on Monday night while carrying Saudi crude from Juaymah. The wider picture is unchanged since the crisis began on February 28: a US-led aerial campaign, a naval blockade of Iran, IRGC warnings forbidding passage, boardings, and sea mines laid in the Strait. And yet WTI FELL 1.12% to 89.994 and Brent 1.20% to 94.485. The reconciling fact is throughput: the US Energy Secretary said over 17 million barrels a day transited on Tuesday, the highest since the conflict started, so the market is now pricing observed flow rather than declared intent. Do not mistake this for de-escalation - crude is still +7.74% on the week, +18.77% on the month and +56.73% year to date, EU gas is +30.31% on the month and German gas +27.72%, and the Bank of Canada said explicitly on Tuesday that there has been little progress reopening the Strait. What has changed is the asymmetry. When the biggest escalation of the war cannot lift the price, the risk premium is fully in the market, and the next large move in crude is more likely to come from a de-escalation headline than from another strike. That has three direct FX consequences. It caps rather than breaks the CAD trade - USD/CAD slowed to -0.11% today from -0.36% yesterday, so the loonie is now running on Macklem rather than on crude, which is the more durable of the two legs but also the one that a weak jobs print tomorrow can damage. It removes the strongest argument for pressing USOIL longs at these levels, hence the conviction cut. And it changes what the energy channel means for the tightening trade: the ECB, BoC, BoE hawks and now the SNB are all responding to an inflation impulse that has already been delivered, so their reaction functions no longer need new escalation to keep working. The one currency where this cuts the other way is the yen, because Japan imports essentially all of its oil - a stalling crude price is a quiet tailwind for a trade balance running at MINUS 634 billion yen, and it removes the main fundamental objection to the BoJ hike now 85-90% priced.
